## esquadro add

Add blueprints to the project.

```
Usage: esquadro add [-no-gen] [-trust] <blueprint>[,<blueprint>...] [dir]

Adds blueprints to the app block of the project in dir (default: the current
directory), with the blueprints they require, and generates. A blueprint is
a built-in name (esquadro blueprint list), a local folder (./blueprints/x)
or a git source (github.com/acme/x@v1). Its options are written commented
out, with their defaults, to change when you need to.

  -no-gen
    	change app.esq only, without generating
  -trust
    	let the hooks of blueprints from git run without asking
```

## esquadro blueprint

List, inspect, update, write and test blueprints.

```
Usage: esquadro blueprint <command> [arguments]

Commands:
  list     list the blueprints you can use, and those the project uses
  info     show what a blueprint does: its options, slots and files
  update   move blueprints from git to the latest commit of their ref
  new      start a blueprint of your own in the project
  test     generate a blueprint's test project and compare it with the expected output

To add a blueprint to the project: esquadro add; to remove one: esquadro remove.
```

### esquadro blueprint list

List the blueprints you can use, and those the project uses.

```
Usage: esquadro blueprint list [dir]

Lists the built-in blueprints, by what they are for. In a project (dir,
default: the current directory), marks those the app uses with *, and lists
its blueprints from folders and git too.
```

### esquadro blueprint info

Show what a blueprint does: its options, slots and files.

```
Usage: esquadro blueprint info <blueprint> [dir]

Shows what a blueprint does, the blueprints it works with, its options,
annotations and slots, and the files it generates. The blueprint is a
built-in name, one of the project's in dir (default: the current directory),
a local folder or a git source.
```

### esquadro blueprint update

Move blueprints from git to the latest commit of their ref.

```
Usage: esquadro blueprint update [-trust] [<blueprint>[,...]] [dir]

Moves the project's blueprints from git (all, or those named) to the commit
their ref points to now, and generates. The lockfile keeps each one at its
commit until then. Built-in blueprints come with esquadro: update esquadro.

  -trust
    	let the hooks of the new commits run without asking
```

### esquadro blueprint new

Start a blueprint of your own in the project.

```
Usage: esquadro blueprint new <name> [dir]

Starts a blueprint of your own in esquadro/blueprints/<name> of the project
in dir (default: the current directory) and adds it to the app: a manifest,
a template for the whole project and one for each entity, code added to the
app's Taskfile, and a test project with what the blueprint generates for
it, which esquadro blueprint test checks. Change them to make it yours.
```

### esquadro blueprint test

Generate a blueprint's test project and compare it with the expected output.

```
Usage: esquadro blueprint test [-update] [blueprint]

Generates the blueprint's test project (testdata/project) in a temporary
folder and compares the files the blueprint wrote with testdata/expected.
The blueprint is a folder, or a name of the project's esquadro/blueprints;
by default, the current folder.

  -update
    	make the generated files the expected ones
```

## esquadro check

Check the project for errors.

```
Usage: esquadro check [dir]

Checks the project in dir (default: the current directory) for syntax and
semantic errors without generating anything. The project is the .esq files
of dir's esquadro/ folder; blueprints are loaded as gen loads them.
```

## esquadro doctor

Check that the tools the project needs are installed.

```
Usage: esquadro doctor [dir]

Checks that the tools esquadro and the project in dir (default: the current
directory) need are installed (Go, git, Task, Docker, sqlc), that the
project checks, and that its generated code is what the model generates;
says how to fix what is not. Outside a project, it checks the tools only.
```

## esquadro env

List and check the project's environment variables.

```
Usage: esquadro env <command> [arguments]

Commands:
  list   list the project's environment variables, by environment
  check  check an environment's .env file against the model

Variables are declared in the model: by blueprints, and in app.esq's env blocks.
```

### esquadro env list

List the project's environment variables, by environment.

```
Usage: esquadro env list [dir]

Lists the environment variables of the project in dir (default: the current
directory): their type, the environments that require them, their value in
each environment from the model, and the blueprint that declares them.
```

### esquadro env check

Check an environment's .env file against the model.

```
Usage: esquadro env check [environment] [dir]

Checks the .env.<environment> file of the project in dir (default: the
current directory), or of every environment, against the model: the
variables the environment requires that have no value, values of the wrong
type, and variables the model does not declare. The process's environment
is not read: it checks what the file and the model give.
```

## esquadro explain

Tell where a generated file came from.

```
Usage: esquadro explain [-C dir] <file>

Tells which blueprint and template generated a file, which blueprints it
replaced, who contributed to its slots, and whether you edited it.

  -C string
    	the project folder (default ".")
```

## esquadro fmt

Format .esq files.

```
Usage: esquadro fmt [-w | -check] [path ...]

Formats .esq files: aligned columns, two-space indentation, comments kept.
A path can be a file or a directory (its .esq files, not subdirectories).
The default path is the project's esquadro/ folder, or the current directory
without one. Prints the result unless -w or -check is given.

  -check
    	list files that are not formatted and exit with status 1, without changing them
  -w	write the result back to the files instead of printing it
```

## esquadro gen

Generate the project.

```
Usage: esquadro gen [-dry-run | -check] [-force] [-update] [-trust] [dir]

Generates the project in dir (default: the current directory) from its .esq
files and blueprints. Generated files you edited are never overwritten
unless -force is given; if any would be, nothing is written. Blueprints from
git stay at the commit the lockfile pins until -update; their hooks run
only once you allow them, for each commit.

  -check
    	write nothing, and exit with status 1 if the files are not what the model generates (for CI)
  -dry-run
    	show what would change, with diffs, without writing anything
  -force
    	overwrite or delete generated files you edited
  -trust
    	let the hooks of blueprints from git run without asking
  -update
    	resolve the versions of blueprints from git again, instead of the commits the lockfile pins
```

## esquadro lsp

Run the language server for editors.

```
Usage: esquadro lsp

Runs the language server an editor starts for .esq files: errors while
you type, the same esquadro check reports, and formatting as esquadro fmt
does. It speaks the Language Server Protocol on stdin and stdout.
```

## esquadro new

Create a project.

```
Usage: esquadro new [-starter name | -blueprints list] [-module path] [-no-git] [-no-gen] <name>

Creates the folder <name> with esquadro/app.esq and generates the project.
Without -starter, the project is the smallest one: the app blueprint, and
git, which makes it a repository with a first commit; add blueprints with
esquadro add. A starter is a project to begin from, with its blueprints
listed in app.esq and an example model:

  api      A JSON API on PostgreSQL, with its contract, docs, image and CI, and a catalog to change.
  worker   A background service on PostgreSQL: jobs on a queue, some on a schedule, worked until it is stopped, with its image and CI.
  cli      A command line tool: commands, configuration and CI, nothing else to start with.

  -blueprints string
    	comma-separated blueprints of the app, instead of a starter (default: app,env)
  -module string
    	Go module path (default: github.com/<git config github.user>/<name>, or example.com/<name>)
  -no-gen
    	write the .esq files only, without generating
  -no-git
    	leave out the git blueprint: no repository, no first commit
  -starter string
    	start from a starter: api, worker, cli
```

## esquadro remove

Remove blueprints from the project.

```
Usage: esquadro remove [-no-gen] [-force] <blueprint>[,<blueprint>...] [dir]

Removes blueprints from the app block of the project in dir (default: the
current directory) and generates: the files they generated go, unless you
edited them (then nothing is written, as with gen); the files esquadro wrote
once for you stay. A blueprint another one requires is not removed. Give
a blueprint by its name, as esquadro blueprint list shows it.

  -force
    	delete the blueprint's generated files even if you edited them
  -no-gen
    	change app.esq only, without generating
```

## esquadro version

Print the esquadro version.

```
esquadro version
```
